topics.title: Failure clinic — The queue is bounded but the retry list is not
topics.summary: A frontend rejects tasks when its queue is full, then appends every rejected task to an unbounded retry vector. The queue’s capacity test passes while process memory still grows without limit. Follow rejected work to its final owner and retention policy. A bound is useful only if overflow does not move into an unbounded neighboring structure.

reading.title: Engineering case — Budget a queue in bytes as well as entries
paragraphs: A queue of 100 requests appears bounded. If each request can own a 10 MiB payload, the queue alone can retain roughly one GiB before accounting for container overhead, in-flight copies, and response buffers. An entry limit is not a byte budget.

For the teaching wire protocol, the 4096-byte frame limit constrains one payload. A 64-peer server therefore has a bounded number of bounded request buffers under its implementation, but the process also owns output buffers, database state, allocator metadata, and library caches. Compute an estimate from the actual ownership graph rather than multiplying one number and calling it a complete memory guarantee.

Admission can reserve both an entry slot and a byte allowance. If either reservation fails, reject before transferring ownership of a large buffer. Release both reservations on every terminal path: normal completion, parsing failure, cancellation, timeout, and shutdown. A leaked reservation can mimic a memory leak by permanently reducing capacity.

Weighted admission creates another issue: a client can understate expected work. Validate declared lengths before allocation and enforce measured limits during processing. For expensive operations, an estimated cost can guide fairness while a hard maximum prevents one inaccurate estimate from consuming unbounded resources.

The durable pending quota also needs a disk perspective. Historical completed rows remain retained, and SQLite indexes and WAL activity contribute bytes beyond the logical input. A process with only ten pending jobs can still run out of disk after retaining millions of completed records.

Test capacity boundaries with exact counts and sizes. Verify that a duplicate submission does not reserve a second durable slot, that rejection leaves prior work intact, and that closing a queue drains accepted values without leaking permits. A stress test should report both admission and completed work so it cannot appear successful by simply buffering more requests.

This case turns “bounded” from an adjective into a measurable contract. Name the resource, unit, owner, release point, and overflow action. Without those five details, a limit in one class can coexist with unbounded growth elsewhere.
